claim: KIF19A is a kinesin-8 motor that accumulates at cilia tips and controls cilium length.
source: The kinesin-8 motor, KIF19A, accumulates at cilia tips and controls cilium length.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known function of KIF19A.

claim: Defective KIF19A leads to hydrocephalus and female infertility because of abnormally elongated cilia.
source: Defective KIF19A leads to hydrocephalus and female infertility because of abnormally elongated cilia.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by previous research cited in the introduction.

claim: KIF19A uniquely possesses dual functions of motility along ciliary microtubules and depolymerization of microtubules among kinesins.
source: Uniquely among kinesins, KIF19A possesses the dual functions of motility along ciliary microtubules and depolymerization of microtubules.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a unique characteristic of KIF19A.

claim: The crystal structure of the KIF19A motor domain was solved.
source: To elucidate the molecular mechanisms of these functions we solved the crystal structure of its motor domain
evidence: The manuscript describes solving the crystal structure at 2.7 Å resolution.

claim: The cryo-electron microscopy structure of KIF19A complexed with a microtubule was determined.
source: To elucidate the molecular mechanisms of these functions we solved the crystal structure of its motor domain and determined its cryo-electron microscopy structure complexed with a microtubule.
evidence: The manuscript describes cryo-EM reconstruction at 7.0 Å resolution.

claim: Features enabling KIF19A's dual function are clustered on its microtubule-binding side.
source: The features of KIF19A that enable its dual function are clustered on its microtubule-binding side.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural analysis throughout the manuscript.

claim: A destabilized switch II coordinates with a destabilized L8 to enable KIF19A to adjust to both straight and curved microtubule protofilaments.
source: Unexpectedly, a destabilized switch II coordinates with a destabilized L8 to enable KIF19A to adjust to both straight and curved microtubule protofilaments.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural and mutational analysis.

claim: The basic clusters of L2 and L12 tether the microtubule.
source: The basic clusters of L2 and L12 tether the microtubule.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by mutational analysis showing decreased MT affinity when these clusters are mutated.

claim: The long L2 with a characteristic acidic-hydrophobic-basic sequence effectively stabilizes the curved conformation of microtubule ends.
source: The long L2 with a characteristic acidic-hydrophobic-basic sequence effectively stabilizes the curved conformation of microtubule ends.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural modeling and mutational analysis.

claim: Most KIFs actively move along the MT toward either the plus or minus end to transport cellular cargoes.
source: Most KIFs, including kinesin-1–kinesin-12 and kinesin-14 subfamily members, actively move along the MT toward either the plus or minus end to transport cellular cargoes, such as protein complexes, vesicles and mRNAs (Hirokawa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Kinesin-13 proteins are not actively motile along MTs but depolymerize MTs from both ends to control MT dynamics.
source: In contrast, kinesin-13 proteins, such as KIF2A and KIF2C, are not actively motile along MTs but depolymerize MTs from both ends to control MT dynamics (Desai et al., 1999; Homma et al., 2003; Ogawa et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Kinesin-13 proteins reach the ends of MTs by passive one-dimensional random diffusion or with the assistance of a MT plus end-tracking protein.
source: Kinesin-13 proteins reach the ends of MTs by a passive one-dimensional random diffusion (Helenius et al., 2006) or with the assistance of a MT plus end-tracking protein (Honnappa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Most kinesin-8 motor proteins play critical roles during the cell division process.
source: Most kinesin-8 motor proteins play critical roles during the cell division process, for example in spindle length regulation (Weaver et al., 2011; Su et al., 2013) or in the control of mitotic chromosome alignment (Kline-Smith and Walczak, 2004; Stumpff et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Kip3p requires its C-terminal tail for MT-binding to prevent its detachment from the MT lattice.
source: The most extensively studied kinesin-8, Kip3p (budding yeast kinesin-8; a homologue of mammalian KIF18), requires its C-terminal tail for MT-binding to prevent its detachment from the MT lattice (Mayr et al., 2011; Stumpff et al., 2011; Su et al., 2011; Weaver et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Kip3p is highly processive (>5 μm).
source: Kip3p is highly processive (>5 μm)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Multiple Kip3ps act cooperatively to mediate length-dependent MT depolymerization.
source: Kip3p is highly processive (>5 μm) and multiple Kip3ps act cooperatively to mediate length-dependent MT depolymerization.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Structural studies of KIF18A showed a bent conformation of the α4 relay helix and important loops.
source: Structural studies of the motor domain of the human kinesin-8, KIF18A, showed a bent conformation of the α4 relay helix and important loops, indicating the structural basis of the multi-tasking kinesin-8 motor (Peters et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: KIF19A functions as a MT-depolymerizing kinesin in the control of cilium length.
source: We recently reported that KIF19A functions as a MT-depolymerizing kinesin in the control of cilium length (Niwa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as previous research by the authors with citation support.

claim: Kif19a-/- mice displayed hydrocephalus and female infertility phenotypes due to abnormally elongated cilia that cannot generate proper fluid flow.
source: Kif19a-/- mice displayed hydrocephalus and female infertility phenotypes due to abnormally elongated cilia that cannot generate proper fluid flow.
evidence: This is stated as previous research by the authors.

claim: Unlike KIF18A, a KIF19A dimer without the tail domain depolymerizes MTs mainly from the plus-end.
source: We also reported that, unlike KIF18A, a KIF19A dimer without the tail domain depolymerizes MTs mainly from the plus-end.
evidence: This is stated as previous research by the authors.

claim: KIF19A possesses the key structural elements for the dual functions of the catalytic motor domain.
source: Therefore, KIF19A possesses the key structural elements for the dual functions of the catalytic motor domain.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from previous findings.

claim: Monomeric KIF19A-353 (353WT) moves toward the plus-end of microtubules.
source: The strongly-labeled MT minus-ends lead the MT gliding, suggesting that the monomeric 353WT moves toward the plus-end
evidence: This is demonstrated by MT gliding assays shown in Figure 1 and Video 1.

claim: MT gliding velocity of monomeric 353WT was 5.3 ± 1.2 nm/s.
source: MT gliding velocity was 5.3 ± 1.2 nm/s (n = 105 MTs from three independent preparations, mean ± SD, Figure 1B and C)
evidence: This is measured data from MT gliding assays.

claim: MT gliding velocity of monomeric 353WT was slower than that of dimeric KIF19A-379 (21 ± 3 nm/s).
source: MT gliding velocity was 5.3 ± 1.2 nm/s (n = 105 MTs from three independent preparations, mean ± SD, Figure 1B and C), which was slower than that of dimeric KIF19A-379 (21 ± 3 nm/s) (Niwa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison of measured data with previously published results.

claim: GMPCPP-MTs were dose-dependently depolymerized by 353WT.
source: GMPCPP-MTs were dose-dependently depolymerized by 353WT (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MT depolymerization assays shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The half-maximal effective concentration for MT depolymerization (EC50) of 353WT was 142 ± 2 nM.
source: The half-maximal effective concentration for MT depolymerization (EC50) was 142 ± 2 nM
evidence: This is measured data from dose-response experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The EC50 of 353WT was approximately half that of KIF19A-379 (253 nM).
source: The half-maximal effective concentration for MT depolymerization (EC50) was 142 ± 2 nM, which was approximately half that of KIF19A-379 (253 nM) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a comparison of measured data.

claim: The KIF19A monomer construct 353WT is a dual function motor that moves along and depolymerizes MTs.
source: Either way, these in vitro experiments collectively indicate that the KIF19A monomer construct, 353WT, is a dual function motor that moves along and depolymerizes MTs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: The crystal structure of KIF19A 353WT was solved at 2.7 Å resolution.
source: We investigated the molecular mechanism of the dual functions of the KIF19A 353WT monomeric motor by solving its crystal structure at 2.7 Å resolution (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated as experimental data with reference to supplementary information.

claim: In the initial structure determination, residues of the switch II helix α4 could not be determined because there was no corresponding density at the usual site.
source: At the initial stage of the 353WT structure determination process, the residues of the switch II helix α4 could not be determined because there was no corresponding density at the site where α4 is usually located at the center of the MT-binding interface (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the initial challenge in structure determination.

claim: An unmodeled helical-like density was found more distant from the KIF19A catalytic core.
source: Instead, we found an unmodeled helical-like density, which was more distant from the KIF19A catalytic core (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes an observation from the electron density map.

claim: Long wavelength X-ray diffraction experiment was performed to investigate the property of the unmodeled density.
source: Long wavelength X-ray diffraction experiment was thus performed to investigate the property of this density (Hendrickson and Teeter, 1981; Dauter et al., 1999), because in the switch II helix α4, one cysteine residue exists.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used.

claim: One strong anomalous signal was detected close to the center of the helical density, corresponding to Cys283.
source: Among them, one strong anomalous signal was detected close to the center of the corresponding helical density (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E). When the Cys283 residue was assigned to this anomalous signal, all the residues in α4 and the following loop L12 were reasonably determined (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This describes the experimental finding that allowed structure determination.

claim: The complete tertiary structure of 353WT was determined with an R-factor of 22.2%.
source: In this way, the complete tertiary structure of 353WT was finally determined with a reasonable decrease of the R-factor to 22.2% (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated as the final result of structure determination.

claim: The overall structure of the KIF19A 353WT motor domain shares a similar triangle-shape with other kinesins.
source: The overall structure of the KIF19A 353WT motor domain shared a similar triangle-shape with other kinesins, which consists of a central β-sheet of eight strands, sandwiched between six α-helices, three on either side (Figure 2A and B) (Sack et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a structural observation with citation support.

claim: Mg2+-ADP was found embedded in the nucleotide-binding pocket of the 353WT atomic structure.
source: In the 353WT atomic structure, Mg2+-ADP was found embedded in the nucleotide-binding pocket.
evidence: This is a structural observation.

claim: Remarkable features of the KIF19A motor domain are concentrated on its MT-binding side and include the long and wide L2 loop, the flexible L8 loop, the disordered α4 helix, and the short α6 helix.
source: In comparison with previously solved motor domains of various KIFs, the remarkable features of the KIF19A motor domain are concentrated on its MT-binding side and include the long and wide L2 loop, the flexible L8 loop, the disordered α4 helix, and the short α6 helix (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a structural observation comparing KIF19A to other kinesins.

claim: Loop L2 is located at the minus-end side of the MT-binding surface and is atypically long.
source: Loop L2 is located at the minus-end side (rear side) of the MT-binding surface and is atypically long.
evidence: This is a structural observation.

claim: Loop L8 is more retracted toward the catalytic core compared with that of kinesin-13.
source: Loop L8, which is the major MT-binding region at the plus-end side, is more retracted toward the catalytic core compared with that of kinesin-13 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a structural comparison observation.

claim: The switch II helix α4 is more distant from the motor domain than those of other kinesins including kinesin-8 KIF18A.
source: The switch II helix α4, which is considered the main contributor to MT-based kinesin motility, is more distant from the motor domain than those of other kinesins including kinesin-8 KIF18A (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is a structural comparison observation.

claim: The first portion of helix α5 is more destabilized in KIF19A compared to other kinesins.
source: In comparison to the other kinesins, the first portion of helix α5 is more destabilized in KIF19A (Figure 2F)
evidence: This is a structural comparison observation.

claim: The loop region between α4 and α5 (L12) is longer in KIF19A due to destabilization of the first portion of helix α5.
source: In comparison to the other kinesins, the first portion of helix α5 is more destabilized in KIF19A (Figure 2F); therefore, the loop region between α4 and α5 (L12) is longer.
evidence: This is an inference from structural observation.

claim: The longer L12 might allow the invasion of a neighboring molecule into the space between α4 and the motor domain in the crystal packing environment, resulting in the distant position of α4.
source: This might allow the invasion of a neighboring molecule into the space between α4 and the motor domain in the crystal packing environment, resulting in the distant position of α4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed structure.

claim: Helix α6 serves as a base for the neck-linker element, which is important for both the regulation of ATPase activity and MT-based kinesin motility.
source: Helix α6 serves as a base for the neck-linker element, which is important for both the regulation of ATPase activity and MT-based kinesin motility (Case et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The reduced length of helix α6 by more than one turn might be caused by the atypical glycine mutation (G341) in helix α6.
source: Its reduced length by more than one turn might be caused by the atypical glycine mutation in helix α6, which is not seen in other typical plus end motors (G341, Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on structural observation.

claim: Glycine has high conformational flexibility and often tends to disrupt the α-helix.
source: Glycine has high conformational flexibility and often tends to disrupt the α-helix
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The glycine at position 341 might affect the conformation of the following neck-linker by terminating α6 prematurely.
source: Glycine has high conformational flexibility and often tends to disrupt the α-helix, which might affect the conformation of the following neck-linker by terminating α6 prematurely.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation.

claim: The alanine mutation in the basic L2 cluster (PC2A: R56A-H58A-R59A-R61A) markedly impaired MT depolymerization.
source: PC2A, L55A and IL2A markedly impaired depolymerization, while I54A had little effect (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MT depolymerization assays.

claim: The L55A mutation markedly impaired MT depolymerization.
source: PC2A, L55A and IL2A markedly impaired depolymerization, while I54A had little effect (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MT depolymerization assays.

claim: The IL2A mutation (I54A-L55A) markedly impaired MT depolymerization.
source: PC2A, L55A and IL2A markedly impaired depolymerization, while I54A had little effect (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MT depolymerization assays.

claim: The I54A mutation had little effect on MT depolymerization.
source: PC2A, L55A and IL2A markedly impaired depolymerization, while I54A had little effect (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MT depolymerization assays.

claim: The mean EC50 value of PC2A for MT depolymerization was 4936 ± 15 nM.
source: The mean EC50 values of 353WT, PC2A and L55A in three independent experiments were 142 ± 2 nM, 4936 ± 15 nM and 409 ± 4 nM, respectively (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is measured data from dose-response experiments.

claim: The mean EC50 value of L55A for MT depolymerization was 409 ± 4 nM.
source: The mean EC50 values of 353WT, PC2A and L55A in three independent experiments were 142 ± 2 nM, 4936 ± 15 nM and 409 ± 4 nM, respectively (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is measured data from dose-response experiments.

claim: The substitution of KIF19A L2 mildly increased the depolymerization activity of KIF18A.
source: The substitution of KIF19A L2 mildly increased the depolymerization activity of KIF18A.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MT depolymerization assays shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The L2 of KIF19A did not make KIF5C a MT depolymerase.
source: In contrast, the L2 of KIF19A did not make KIF5C a MT depolymerase.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MT depolymerization assays shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The basic cluster of L2 and Leu 55 at the tip of L2 play crucial roles in depolymerization from MT ends.
source: These data collectively suggested that the basic cluster of L2, as well as the Leu 55 at the tip of L2, play crucial roles in depolymerization from MT ends
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis data.

claim: Simple swapping of L2 is not sufficient for transport motors such as KIF5C to attain MT depolymerization function.
source: although the simple swapping of L2 is not sufficient for transport motors such as KIF5C to attain MT depolymerization function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the swap mutant data.

claim: The basal ATPase activities of 353WT, L55A, and PC2A in the absence of MTs or tubulins were all comparable to that of Kip3p.
source: The basal ATPase activities of 353WT, L55A, and PC2A in the absence of MTs or tubulins were all comparable to that of another kinesin-8 motor, Kip3p (Figures 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (Gupta et al., 2006).
evidence: This is measured data from ATPase assays with citation comparison.

claim: Activation of 353WT by MTs caused the ATPase to be activated ~300 times to reach a maximum rate of 1.43 ± 0.07 s−1.
source: Activation of 353WT by MTs caused the ATPase to be activated ~300 times to reach a maximum rate of 1.43 ± 0.07 s−1
evidence: This is measured data from ATPase assays.

claim: Free tubulin-dimers caused the 353WT ATPase to be activated ~200 times to reach a maximum rate of 0.80 ± 0.06 s−1.
source: while free tubulin-dimers caused the ATPase to be activated ~200 times to reach a maximum rate of 0.80 ± 0.06 s−1 (Figures 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is measured data from ATPase assays.

claim: The KIF19A ATPase is similarly activated by both MTs and tubulins.
source: Thus, the KIF19A ATPase is similarly activated by both MTs and tubulins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ATPase data.

claim: The characteristic of ATPase activation by both MTs and tubulins is conserved among kinesin-8 proteins, including KIF18A.
source: This characteristic is conserved among kinesin-8 proteins, including KIF18A (Peters et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The ratio of KIF19A ATPase activation by tubulins/MTs is much higher than that of KIF18A.
source: However, the ratio of KIF19A ATPase activation by tubulins/MTs is much higher than that of KIF18A
evidence: This is a comparison with cited data.

claim: KIF19A is more adapted to tubulins to increase MT depolymerization activity compared to KIF18A.
source: suggesting that KIF19A is more adapted to tubulins to increase MT depolymerization activity.
evidence: This is an inference from the ATPase data comparison.

claim: L55A exhibited relatively small effects on ATPase turnover in the absence or presence of MTs or tubulins compared to KIF19A 353WT.
source: Compared to KIF19A 353WT, L55A exhibited relatively small effects on ATPase turnover in the absence or presence of MTs (Figures 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), or in the presence of tubulins (Figures 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is measured data from ATPase assays.

claim: The affinities for MTs and tubulins were slightly affected by the L55A mutation.
source: The affinities for MTs and tubulins were slightly affected by the L55A mutation (Figure 4A and 4B).
evidence: This is measured data from binding assays.

claim: The role of L55 in MT depolymerization is independent from that of the KIF19A catalytic cycle stimulated by MTs or tubulins.
source: This indicates that the role of L55 in MT depolymerization is independent from that of the KIF19A catalytic cycle stimulated by MTs or tubulins.
evidence: This is an inference from the mutational analysis data.

claim: The L55 property seems similar to that of the valine residue of the KVD finger in kinesin-13.
source: This L55 property seems similar to that of the valine residue of the KVD finger in kinesin-13 (Ogawa et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a comparison with cited data.

claim: PC2A significantly decreased the MT/tubulin stimulation of the KIF19A ATPase.
source: In contrast, PC2A significantly decreased the MT/tubulin stimulation of the KIF19A ATPase (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is measured data from ATPase assays.

claim: The PC2A mutation did not significantly affect the KM, tubulin, but markedly increased the KM, MT to approximately 30 times that of 353WT.
source: The PC2A mutation did not significantly affect the KM, tubulin, but markedly increased the KM, MT to approximately 30 times that of 353WT (Figures 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is measured data from ATPase kinetics assays.

claim: The basic residues in L2 might strengthen the MT-lattice binding at the weak-binding state, similar to the K-loop of KIF1A.
source: suggesting that the basic residues in L2 might strengthen the MT-lattice binding at the weak-binding state, similar to the K-loop of KIF1A (Okada and Hirokawa, 2000).
evidence: This is an inference from the kinetics data with citation comparison.

claim: The PC2A mutation decreased the ATPase stimulation by tubulin without affecting the KM, tubulin.
source: The PC2A mutation also decreased the ATPase stimulation by tubulin without affecting the KM, tubulin.
evidence: This is measured data from ATPase assays.

claim: The KIF19A-specific basic residues of L2 might be involved in the tubulin-activated ATPase pathway.
source: Hence, the KIF19A-specific basic residues of L2 might be involved in the tubulin-activated ATPase pathway, as described later.
evidence: This is an inference from the ATPase data.

claim: L55A slightly decreased MT affinity (Kd, MT 1.6 ± 0.3 μM) compared to 353WT (Kd, MT 0.6 ± 0.1 μM).
source: We found that L55A slightly decreased MT affinity (353WT, Kd, MT 0.6 ± 0.1 μM; L55A, Kd, MT 1.6 ± 0.3 μM)
evidence: This is measured data from MT co-sedimentation assays.

claim: PC2A severely decreased MT affinity (Kd,MT 5.8 ± 2.1 μM).
source: whereas PC2A severely decreased MT affinity (PC2A, Kd,MT 5.8 ± 2.1 μM), consistent with the kinetics data above (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is measured data from MT co-sedimentation assays.

claim: The speed of the L55A mutant MT gliding was 7.5 ± 0.6 nm/s, a little higher than that of 353WT.
source: The speed of the L55A mutant was a little higher than that of 353WT described above (L55A, 7.5 ± 0.6 nm/s, Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is measured data from MT gliding assays.

claim: Bound MTs were rarely detected when the PC2A mutant was fixed on the coverslip at the same concentration as L55A.
source: However, bound MTs were rarely detected when the PC2A mutant, at the same concentration as L55A, was fixed on the coverslip.
evidence: This is an observation from MT gliding assays.

claim: Increasing the concentration of PC2A (1 mg/ml) enabled sufficient microtubules to fix to the glass surface.
source: Although PC2A bound fewer MTs than 353WT, increasing the concentration of PC2A (1 mg/ml) enabled sufficient microtubules to fix to the glass surface (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from MT binding assays.

claim: Bound MTs glided distances that were too short to reliably calculate the gliding speed on the PC2A-coated coverslip.
source: Even in these conditions, however, bound MTs glided distances that were too short to reliably calculate the gliding speed on the PC2A-coated coverslip.
evidence: This is an observation from MT gliding assays.

claim: The L2 of KIF19A, especially its basic cluster, is necessary for 353WT to stay attached to MTs.
source: indicating that the L2 of KIF19A, especially its basic cluster, is necessary for 353WT to stay attached to MTs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis data.

claim: MTs glided much more slowly with the KIF18A swap mutant (10.2 ± 0.1 nm/s) compared with KIF18A WT (34.4 ± 0.3 nm/s).
source: As a consequence, MTs glided much more slowly with the swap mutants compared with the wild-type motors (KIF18A WT, 34.4 ± 0.3 nm/s; KIF18A swap, 10.2 ± 0.1 nm/s
evidence: This is measured data from MT gliding assays.

claim: MTs glided much more slowly with the KIF5C swap mutant (68.9 ± 0.2 nm/s) compared with KIF5C WT (179.9 ± 2.5 nm/s).
source: KIF5C WT, 179.9 ± 2.5 nm/s; KIF5C swap, 68.9 ± 0.2 nm/s) (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: This is measured data from MT gliding assays.

claim: The intensive ionic interactions between the L2 of KIF19A and MTs might reduce motility speed.
source: The intensive ionic interactions between the L2 of KIF19A and MTs might reduce motility speed.
evidence: This is an inference from the swap mutant data.

claim: KIF19A L2 is likely to interact electrostatically with the MT to tether the KIF19A motor domain on the MT, which in turn reduces motility speed on the MT.
source: KIF19A L2 is thus likely to interact electrostatically with the MT to tether the KIF19A motor domain on the MT, which in turn reduces motility speed on the MT.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational and swap data.

claim: The most remarkable structural difference between KIF19A and other kinesins was found in the switch II region, α4-L12-α5, which is destabilized and distant from the motor domain.
source: The most remarkable structural difference between KIF19A and other kinesins was found in the switch II region, α4-L12-α5, which is destabilized and distant from the motor domain (Figures 2A–B and 5B).
evidence: This is a structural observation.

claim: The KIF18A L12 swap mutant slightly increased soluble tubulin compared to 353WT.
source: In comparison to 353WT, soluble tubulin was decreased in the presence of KIF5C L12, but was slightly increased in the presence of KIF18A L12 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is measured data from MT depolymerization assays.

claim: The KIF5C L12 swap mutant decreased soluble tubulin compared to 353WT.
source: In comparison to 353WT, soluble tubulin was decreased in the presence of KIF5C L12, but was slightly increased in the presence of KIF18A L12 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is measured data from MT depolymerization assays.

claim: KIF18A L12 has three continuous basic residues (K299, R300 and R301).
source: Within the KIF18A L12 sequence, three continuous basic residues (K299, R300 and R301) are present.
evidence: This is a sequence observation.

claim: KIF5C L12 has only one basic residue, K274.
source: Only one basic residue, K274, was found in the L12 of KIF5C
evidence: This is a sequence observation.

claim: KIF19A L12 has two basic residues, K290 and K294.
source: whereas two basic residues, K290 and K294, were found in the L12 of KIF19A.
evidence: This is a sequence observation.

claim: GS2R exhibited a slight increase in MT depolymerization activity, similar to the KIF18A L2 swap mutant.
source: As expected, GS2R exhibited a slight increase in MT depolymerization activity, similar to the KIF18A L2 swap mutant
evidence: This is measured data from MT depolymerization assays.

claim: K2A without basic residues in L12 showed lower MT depolymerization ability, similar to the KIF5C L2 swap mutant.
source: whereas K2A without basic residues in L12 showed lower MT depolymerization ability, similar to the KIF5C L2 swap mutant (Figure 5D–G).
evidence: This is measured data from MT depolymerization assays.

claim: The mean EC50 value of GS2R for MT depolymerization was 91 ± 2 nM.
source: The mean EC50 values of 353WT, GS2R and K2A were 142 ± 2 nM, 91 ± 2 nM and 678 ± 5 nM, respectively.
evidence: This is measured data from dose-response experiments.

claim: The mean EC50 value of K2A for MT depolymerization was 678 ± 5 nM.
source: The mean EC50 values of 353WT, GS2R and K2A were 142 ± 2 nM, 91 ± 2 nM and 678 ± 5 nM, respectively.
evidence: This is measured data from dose-response experiments.

claim: The depolymerization speed of GS2R was 30.0 ± 4.9 nm/s.
source: The depolymerization speeds of 353WT, GS2R and K2A were 10.9 ± 2.0 nm/s, 30.0 ± 4.9 nm/s, and 2.0 ± 0.5 nm/s, respectively.
evidence: This is measured data from TIRF microscopy observations.

claim: The depolymerization speed of K2A was 2.0 ± 0.5 nm/s.
source: The depolymerization speeds of 353WT, GS2R and K2A were 10.9 ± 2.0 nm/s, 30.0 ± 4.9 nm/s, and 2.0 ± 0.5 nm/s, respectively.
